title: Can You Love Jesus and Still Struggle With Lust?
paragraphs:
Can You Love Jesus and Still Struggle With Lust?
The Question That Terrifies Countless Christians—And the Gospel Answer That Can Set You Free
There are battles many Christians talk about openly.
Anxiety.
Fear.
Doubt.
Grief.
But there is one battle that often stays hidden behind forced smiles, raised hands during worship, and carefully rehearsed prayers.
Lust.
For countless believers, the greatest fear isn't simply falling into temptation.
It's wondering whether their struggle means they never truly loved Jesus in the first place.
"If I really loved Christ... why do I still battle this?"
"If the Holy Spirit lives in me... why does this temptation keep returning?"
"Am I a hypocrite?"
"Have I disappointed God too many times?"
If you've ever whispered those questions through tears, this article is for you.
Not to excuse sin.
Not to minimize holiness.
But to let the light of God's Word speak louder than the accusations of shame.
Because our theme has always been true:
The Bible never hides the reality that genuine believers still wrestle with the flesh. In fact, one of the strongest examples comes from the apostle Paul himself.
In Romans 7:15, Paul writes:
The Greek text reads:
ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω· οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ᾽ ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ.
(Ho gar katergazomai ou ginōskō; ou gar ho thelō touto prassō, all' ho misō touto poiō.)
Notice something remarkable.
Paul doesn't say he loves his sin.
He says he hates it.
That difference matters.
Very much.
Lust becomes especially dangerous when we stop fighting it.
The struggle itself is not proof that Christ has abandoned you.
The hatred of sin, the grief over falling, the longing to obey Jesus—those are evidences of a heart the Holy Spirit is transforming.
Scripture never teaches that Christians become incapable of temptation.
Jesus Himself "has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15).
Temptation is not sin.
Entertaining it.
Feeding it.
Choosing it.
Those are different matters.
James explains the progression with sobering clarity.
James 1:14–15 says:
"But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death."
The Greek word translated "desire" is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia).
It simply means a powerful longing or craving.
The word itself is neutral depending on context.
Jesus even said in Luke 22:15,
ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα
"I have earnestly desired..."
The same word can describe holy longing or sinful craving.
Lust is not merely attraction.
God created beauty.
God created marriage.
God created sexual intimacy.
Genesis repeatedly declares creation טוֹב (ṭov)—"good."
Sin did not create sexuality.
Sin corrupted it.
Lust takes what God designed as covenant love and turns another human being into an object for self-gratification.
Jesus addressed the heart directly in Matthew 5:28.
"But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
The phrase "with lustful intent" translates the Greek:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
(pros to epithymēsai autēn)
Jesus isn't condemning the involuntary recognition that someone is attractive.
He exposes the intentional cultivation of desire that seeks to possess another person in the heart apart from God's design.
The issue is not merely the eyes.
It is worship.
Every act of lust asks the soul to believe one dangerous lie:
"This pleasure will satisfy me more than Christ."
That is why lust is ultimately not only a moral issue.
It is a worship issue.
Yet here is the astonishing beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come only for people who had already conquered their sins.
He came for sinners who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 reminds us:
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after you finally won every battle.
Not after you cleaned yourself up.
While you were still a sinner.
The enemy loves to whisper,
"You failed again. Don't pray today."
Jesus says,
"Come."
The enemy says,
"God is tired of forgiving you."
Jesus says,
"Whoever comes to me I will never cast out." (John 6:37)
The Greek is breathtakingly emphatic:
οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω
(ou mē ekbalō exō)
"I will certainly never cast out."
The double negative οὐ μὴ is among the strongest ways Greek expresses absolute certainty.
Jesus isn't reluctant to receive repentant sinners.
He promises it.
Real repentance is not merely feeling guilty after getting caught.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια (metanoia).
Literally, it means a change of mind that results in a transformed direction of life.
Repentance does not mean you never stumble again.
It means every time you fall, you run toward Christ instead of away from Him.
Peter fell.
David fell.
The Corinthian believers struggled deeply.
Yet God continued His redeeming work because grace does not excuse sin—it transforms sinners.
This is why Galatians 5 describes the Christian life as a conflict.
"For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh."
The Christian life is not evidence of the absence of war.
It is evidence that the war has begun.
Before Christ, many people sinned without conviction.
After Christ, the Spirit produces holy discomfort because He refuses to leave His children unchanged.
That discomfort is painful.
But it is also hopeful.
Dead hearts don't fight sin.
Living hearts do.
Perhaps you've promised God a thousand times that this would be the last failure.
Perhaps you've deleted apps.
Installed accountability software.
Made resolutions.
Only to stumble again.
Do not misunderstand this encouragement.
Take radical steps against temptation.

Jesus' language about cutting off a hand or plucking out an eye (Matthew 5:29–30) is hyperbolic imagery emphasizing decisive action against sin. We are never called to harm ourselves physically, but we are called to remove whatever consistently draws us into sin. If a device, habit, relationship, or environment repeatedly feeds lust, wisdom and obedience may require letting it go.
But remember this:
Your greatest hope is not your self-discipline.
It is your Savior.

Sanctification is God's ongoing work of conforming believers to Christ (Philippians 1:6). Growth is often gradual. Some victories come quickly; others unfold through years of dependence on God's grace, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, confession, accountability, and the Spirit's power. Our confidence rests not in our perfection but in God's faithfulness to complete what He has begun.
Maybe today you needed permission to stop pretending.
Maybe you've been exhausted from wearing a mask at church.
Maybe you thought everyone else had already figured out holiness while you silently drowned.
You're not alone.
The answer to the question,
"Can you love Jesus and still struggle with lust?"
is not permission to remain in sin.
It is an invitation to distinguish between a heart that clings to sin and a heart that clings to Christ while fighting sin.

Followers of Jesus are called to pursue purity with seriousness, relying daily on God's grace. If your struggle has led you to repentance, dependence on Christ, confession, and a desire to obey Him, do not confuse the battle with abandonment. Keep bringing every failure into the light, trusting that "if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

If this article reminded you that God's grace is greater than your shame, consider sharing it so that someone silently fighting the same battle can encounter the hope of Christ. Your testimony may encourage another believer who feels alone.
Because someone else's freedom may begin with the courage you show by sharing hope today.
